results.request: Design a small invoice ingestion service for one server and two developers, about 2000 invoices/day. Clients retry submissions after timeouts. Keep existing SQLite storage. No implementation requested. Give components, data ownership, failure handling and one alternative with tradeoffs.
results.rawAnswer: {"summary":"Design-only answer. Assumptions labeled; no implementation, no benchmarks invented.","assumptions":["~2000 invoices/day = ~0.023/s average, bursty (batch uploads at month end). SQLite is not a throughput constraint at this scale; the real constraints are duplicate delivery from client retries, crash recovery, and 2-developer maintainability.","'Keep existing SQLite storage' means one file on the same server; no Postgres, no external broker.","Clients can be asked to send an idempotency key; if they cannot, content-hash fallback is used (labeled weaker).","No compliance/PII constraints stated; if invoices contain PII, add encryption-at-rest and retention decisions."],"components":[{"name":"Ingest API (thin, synchronous)","responsibility":"Auth, schema validation, idempotency-key resolution, one fast SQLite write, return 202 + submission_id. Target <50 ms so client timeouts are rare. No parsing, no business rules, no network calls to third parties on the request path."},{"name":"Processor (worker)","responsibility":"Claims pending submissions, parses/normalizes invoice, applies business validation, writes the invoice record, marks status. Runs as an in-process background task (or a second systemd unit if you prefer isolation). Retries with exponential backoff, dead-letters after N attempts."},{"name":"SQLite (WAL)","responsibility":"Single source of durable truth. journal_mode=WAL, busy_timeout, synchronous=NORMAL, one writer connection (or one writer process), foreign_keys=ON. WAL lets readers (status queries, reporting) run concurrently with the writer."},{"name":"Status/ops surface","responsibility":"GET /submissions/{id} for clients to resolve timeout ambiguity; /healthz; counters (accepted, duplicate, processed, failed, dead-lettered, queue depth); systemd restart; nightly `VACUUM INTO`/`.backup` file copy; log rotation."}],"data_ownership":{"invoice_submissions":"Owned by Ingest API. Append-only intake ledger: submission_id, idempotency_key (UNIQUE), payload or payload_hash, received_at, status(pending|processing|done|failed|dead), attempts, claimed_at/lease_expires, last_error. API is the only writer of new rows.","invoices":"Owned by Processor. Normalized, business-validated output; FK to submission_id. API never writes here.","idempotency ledger":"Same table as submissions via UNIQUE(idempotency_key); API owns conflict resolution.","audit/events":"Owned by Processor (state transitions), for replay and debugging.","Rule: exactly one writer process against the SQLite file at a time. If the worker is a separate process, serialize writes through a single connection or a claim-then-write protocol; SQLite tolerates one writer plus many readers, not two concurrent writers."],"request_flow_representative_case":["Client POSTs invoice with Idempotency-Key: abc. API validates, INSERTs submission (status=pending) in one transaction, returns 202 + submission_id.","Client times out before receiving the response and retries with the same key. INSERT hits UNIQUE conflict; API returns the existing submission_id with 200 and its current status. No duplicate invoice is possible.","Processor claims the row via an atomic status transition (pending -> processing with lease), parses, validates, writes invoice, sets status=done.","If the client still needs certainty, it polls GET /submissions/{id} until done or failed."],"failure_handling":{"duplicate_retry":"UNIQUE(idempotency_key) + INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING/RETURNING existing row. Key reuse with a different payload_hash returns 409 rather than silently accepting.","timeout_mid_write":"SQLite transactions are atomic: the submission row either exists or does not. Retry is always safe; the idempotency key is the dedupe boundary, not the HTTP response.","worker_crash":"Lease columns (claimed_at, lease_expires). A reaper resets expired leases back to pending. Processing must be idempotent per submission_id (delete-or-upsert invoice for that submission_id) so a re-run after a partial write is safe.","poison_invoice":"Bounded attempts (e.g. 5) with exponential backoff, then status=dead with last_error and an alert. Manual replay endpoint re-queues it after a fix. Never an infinite retry loop that starves the queue.","disk_full_or_locked":"busy_timeout plus explicit SQLITE_BUSY handling -> 503 with Retry-After; healthcheck fails on write probe so systemd/monitoring reacts.","backup_recovery":"Nightly online backup to a separate file, retained N days; restore is copy-file + restart. Test the restore once per quarter."],"observability_and_test_hooks":["Queue depth (pending count) and oldest-pending age are the two alerts that matter at this scale.","Duplicate rate metric tells you whether client timeouts are actually happening.","Test the important assumption cheaply: replay the same idempotency key 1000x concurrently and assert exactly one invoice row; kill -9 the worker mid-claim and assert the row is re-processed exactly once."],"recommended_design":"Single deployable process (or two systemd units) on one server: thin ingest + in-process worker + SQLite WAL + submission ledger. Simplest thing that makes retries safe and recovery automatic; one codebase, one language, one deploy artifact for two developers.","alternative":{"name":"File-drop / spool directory instead of a queue table","description":"Ingest API writes each submission to an append-only spool file (or accepts uploads into an inbox directory); a worker consumes files in order and records results in SQLite. SQLite then stores only final invoices plus a processed-keys index.","pros":["Removes SQLite write contention entirely; the filesystem is the durable queue and is trivially inspectable with ls.","Crash-safe by construction (write temp file, atomic rename); easy manual replay by re-dropping a file.","Backpressure is visible on disk; no lease/reaper code."],"cons":["Two durable stores (files + SQLite) that can disagree; you need a reconciliation pass to detect 'file consumed but DB write failed'.","Ordering, partial files, and cross-device rename semantics are subtle; no transactional atomicity between 'file consumed' and 'invoice inserted'.","Harder to query state ('what is pending right now?') without scanning the directory; status endpoint needs the processed-keys index.","More moving parts to reason about for two developers than a single queue table."],"verdict":"Prefer the SQLite submission ledger: it keeps one durable store, gives transactional atomicity between intake and dedupe, and makes status queries trivial. results.request: Propose a minimal repair of this JavaScript helper; the public contract is an inclusive integer range and an empty array when start > end. Existing function: function range(start,end){return Array.from({length:Math.max(0,end-start)},(_,i)=>start+i)}. Return the replacement function in a code field and representative checks. Do not claim files were edited or tests executed.

answer.diagnosis: Off-by-one: `end - start` undercounts by one for an inclusive range, so range(1,3) yields [1,2] instead of [1,2,3]. The `Math.max(0, ...)` guard already satisfies the empty-array-when-start>end contract, so the minimal fix is to add `+ 1` to the length expression.
answer.diffSummary: Single-token change: `Math.max(0, end - start)` -> `Math.max(0, end - start + 1)`. Signature, name, return type (Array of numbers), and the start > end -> [] behavior are unchanged; no new dependencies or abstractions.

checks.covers: guard prevents negative Array.from length (which would throw RangeError)

answer.verificationStatus: Not executed. No files were edited and no tests were run in this environment; the checks above are proposed assertions derived from the stated contract, intended to be run with the project's existing test runner (or a plain `node -e` / console.assert smoke check).
answer.limitationsAndOptions: The contract specifies an integer range, so non-integer inputs (e.g. range(0, 2.5) -> [0,1,2]) and non-numeric inputs (NaN -> []) are out of scope for a minimal repair. If callers may pass floats or non-numbers, add validation at this owning layer (e.g. Number.isSafeInteger checks or a `throw new TypeError`) as a separate, explicitly scoped change rather than folding it into this fix. Also note the function allocates the full array eagerly; for very large ranges a generator/iterator would be preferable, but that changes the public contract and is therefore out of scope here.

  "findings": [
    {
      "severity": "critical",
      "location": "api/profile.js:1 (`const key=req.params.id` / `cache.has(key)`)",
      "issue": "Cache key is not tenant-scoped, so the tenant filter on the DB query is bypassed on cache hits.",
      "trigger": "Tenant A requests profile id=X (miss) → row cached under key `X`. Tenant B then requests id=X → `cache.has(key)` is true and tenant A's row is returned without any DB call, so `tenantId` is never checked.",
      "consequence": "Cross-tenant data exposure (IDOR). The stated invariant 'every query applies the tenant filter' is true for the DB but not for the response path; the cache becomes an unauthenticated cross-tenant read channel.",
      "remedy": "Include the tenant in the key (e.g. `${req.auth.tenantId}:${id}`) or namespace per-tenant caches; never key on a client-supplied id alone."
    },
    {
      "severity": "high",
      "location": "api/profile.js:1 (`cache.set(key,row)` when `findFirst` returns null)",
      "issue": "Misses/negatives are cached and never expire, and are also shared across tenants.",
      "trigger": "Tenant B requests id=X that exists only in tenant A → `findFirst` returns null → null cached under `X`. Tenant A later requests id=X → served the cached null. Separately, a row created after a first miss is permanently invisible.",
      "consequence": "Permanent false 'not found' for legitimate rows, plus a cross-tenant existence oracle (an attacker can probe which ids other tenants have already cached as null).",
      "remedy": "Do not cache nulls, or cache them with a short TTL and tenant-scoped key."
    },
    {
      "severity": "high",
      "location": "api/profile.js:1 (`const cache=new Map()`)",
      "issue": "Unbounded, never-invalidated, process-local cache.",

    },

      "location": "api/profile.js:1 (`if(cache.has(key)) ... cache.get(key)`)",

      "trigger": "N concurrent requests for the same cold key.",

    }

The provider may have accepted the first attempt, and two workers can process the same order concurrently. Existing tests only mock a single successful call. Give meaningful unit/integration checks and distinguish planned checks from executed evidence; no tests have run here.

assumptionsToConfirm: provider exposes an idempotency key or client-side request reference
order row has a state column and/or unique constraint usable for fencing
worker retry policy: attempt count, backoff, and whether retry reuses the same idempotency key

plannedChecks.setup: fake provider raises read-timeout on attempt 1, succeeds on attempt 2
plannedChecks.assert: worker returns success, provider called exactly 2 times, same idempotency key on both calls
plannedChecks.why: pins retry-on-timeout and key reuse; current mock never fails

plannedChecks.setup: provider times out with no response body
plannedChecks.assert: worker marks order RECONCILE_PENDING (or queries status endpoint) before charging again; no second charge without confirmation
plannedChecks.why: the core money-safety rule: timeout means 'unknown', not 'not charged'

plannedChecks.name: retry_budget_and_backoff
plannedChecks.assert: exactly N attempts, bounded backoff, terminal state FAILED_WITH_RECONCILE, no infinite loop
plannedChecks.why: prevents retry storms and duplicate exposure

plannedChecks.name: non_retryable_error_not_retried
plannedChecks.assert: single call, no retry, no reconcile

plannedChecks.name: provider_accepted_first_attempt_visible_via_status_lookup
plannedChecks.setup: attempt 1 times out; status endpoint reports CAPTURED
plannedChecks.assert: worker records success from lookup, never re-charges

plannedChecks.name: duplicate_delivery_single_charge
plannedChecks.setup: real DB + fake provider; same order dispatched to two workers concurrently (barrier start)
plannedChecks.assert: provider charge endpoint invoked exactly once; order row terminal state unique; second worker observes in-flight/claimed state and exits
plannedChecks.why: directly tests the two-worker race the current suite cannot see

plannedChecks.name: db_level_idempotency_guard
plannedChecks.setup: force both workers past the app-level check (e.g. injected sleep after read)
plannedChecks.assert: unique index on (order_id, idempotency_key) or atomic state transition (UPDATE ... WHERE status='PENDING') admits exactly one winner; second insert raises and is handled
plannedChecks.why: proves the invariant is enforced by storage, not only by application logic

plannedChecks.name: crash_between_charge_and_record
plannedChecks.setup: worker charges, then dies before persisting; restart re-runs
plannedChecks.assert: reconcile path finds the capture and completes the order without a second charge
plannedChecks.why: timeout + crash is the realistic duplicate-capture path

plannedChecks.name: stale_worker_fencing
plannedChecks.setup: worker A stalls, times out its lease, worker B completes; A resumes and writes
plannedChecks.assert: A's write is rejected (lease/version token), final state remains B's

plannedChecks.name: provider_idempotency_semantics
plannedChecks.assert: same key twice returns the original capture, not a new one; timeout fixture returns no body
plannedChecks.why: our safety depends on provider behaviour; verify, don't assume

plannedChecks.name: user_sees_one_charge_after_timeout
plannedChecks.assert: one ledger entry, one provider capture, order marked paid

results.request: User reports host CPU saturation. The only observation is ps inside Codali sandbox showing two processes. There is no host diagnostic connector. Explain what this evidence establishes, whether it disproves host saturation, and the next useful evidence to request. Do not invent host metrics.

answer.question: Does a sandbox `ps` showing two processes bear on the reported host CPU saturation?

scope_of_observation.what_was_run: ps inside the Codali sandbox (isolated run_shell)
scope_of_observation.observed: two processes visible at one instant
scope_of_observation.namespace: sandbox PID namespace / cgroup, not the host
scope_of_observation.connector_status: no host diagnostic connector available — this capability is missing, not negative evidence

what_the_evidence_establishes: The sandbox's own process table contained two entries at that timestamp.
The observation boundary is the sandbox, so any conclusion drawn from it is limited to the sandbox view.

The sandbox is not itself running a large number of visible userland processes at that moment, so the sandbox is an unlikely sole source of a sustained CPU storm (weak, not conclusive: thread count, CPU time and cgroup quota were not measured).
A single `ps` snapshot is a point-in-time listing, not a rate; it carries no utilization, load, or duration information.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not disprove host CPU saturation. It is non-discriminating: the same two-process output is equally consistent with an idle host and with a host pegged at 100%.

Host processes, threads, kernel time, soft/hard IRQ, and other containers are outside this PID namespace and cgroup view, so their absence from the output is an artifact of scope, not proof of absence.
A snapshot cannot show sustained saturation; saturation is a rate over a time window.
It does not distinguish CPU utilization from load average (run-queue depth can be high while per-CPU percent looks moderate, or vice versa), nor user CPU from iowait/steal.
It says nothing about whether the sandbox itself is CPU-quota-throttled, which would further distort any sandbox-local view.

next_useful_evidence_to_request.prerequisite: A host-scoped measurement path: a host diagnostic connector, a host shell, or the user running commands on the affected machine themselves.
confirm_the_boundary_first: systemd-detect-virt; cat /proc/1/cgroup — prove the command is executing on the host, not in a container.
uptime / server_time — anchor the timestamp to the reported symptom window.
measure_the_rate_over_an_interval: vmstat 1 10 or mpstat -P ALL 1 5 — per-CPU user/system/iowait/steal over a window, not one sample.
cat /proc/pressure/cpu twice ~5s apart — direct CPU-pressure stall evidence.
uptime — 1/5/15-minute load average versus core count (nproc).
identify_the_consumers: ps -eo pid,ppid,pcpu,pmem,nlwp,etime,comm --sort=-pcpu | head -20 — top CPU consumers including thread counts.
systemd-cgtop -m cpu or cgroup v2 cpu.stat — attribute burn to a service/container rather than a single process.
top -b -n 1 with per-CPU lines, or btop, for a visual breakdown.
rule_out_adjacent_causes: iostat -x 1 5 / vmstat wa column — iowait masquerading as CPU pressure.
dmesg --ctime | tail, or journalctl -k — thermal throttling, frequency limits, OOM/soft lockups.
lscpu / cat /sys/fs/cgroup/**/cpu.max — host core count and any quota or steal from a hypervisor.
define_the_symptom: Which application or endpoint, what latency/error signature, exact start time, and whether it is continuous or bursty — so the measurement window can be aligned to the event.

answer.method_note: Per the system-diagnostics workflow: state observations, likely causes, and the next discriminating check separately; do not treat one snapshot as proof of sustained performance; do not infer host state from a sandbox view; do not change service or cgroup configuration to collect data. No host metrics have been measured or asserted here.
answer.conclusion: The two-process sandbox `ps` establishes only the sandbox's own process visibility at one instant. It neither confirms nor refutes host CPU saturation. The decisive next step is obtaining host-scoped, interval-based CPU measurements (vmstat/mpstat/sar, PSI, load average vs core count) plus top-consumer and cgroup attribution, after verifying the command actually runs on the host.
